reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: The commonest inherited kidney disease, characterised by progressive bilateral renal cyst formation and enlarging kidneys
Most disease results from mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1); PKD2 (polycystin-2) disease is generally milder with later kidney failure
Typical presentations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, haematuria, urinary tract infection, stones, or an incidental family finding
Extrarenal features include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve abnormalities and abdominal wall or inguinal hernias
Diagnosis is usually by ultrasound using age-adjusted cyst-count criteria in an at-risk individual, with genetic testing where imaging is equivocal
Total kidney volume is a validated marker of disease progression and helps identify rapid progressors
Blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin blockade and, in selected rapidly progressing patients, a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist can slow decline
reference.pathophysiology: ADPKD is caused by heterozygous mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, proteins that localise to the primary cilium and regulate tubular cell proliferation, differentiation and fluid secretion. A somatic second hit in individual tubular cells is thought to trigger focal cyst initiation, and cysts then expand through cell proliferation and fluid secretion driven in part by cyclic AMP and vasopressin signalling. Progressive cyst growth distorts and compresses the surrounding parenchyma, causing interstitial fibrosis, activation of the renin-angiotensin system, hypertension and gradual loss of glomerular filtration over decades.
additionalDifferentials: Simple renal cysts or acquired cystic disease of chronic kidney disease
Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal cysts and angiomyolipomas
Von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cysts and tumours
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound applying age-specific cyst-number diagnostic criteria
MRI or CT for total kidney volume measurement and prognostication
Blood pressure assessment and renal function monitoring
Urinalysis for haematuria, proteinuria and infection
MR angiography screening for intracranial aneurysm in selected patients (family history or high-risk occupation)
Genetic testing of PKD1 and PKD2 when imaging is inconclusive or for family or reproductive planning
redFlags: Sudden severe headache suggesting rupture of an intracranial aneurysm
Cyst infection or haemorrhage with fever, severe pain or sepsis
Rapidly rising blood pressure or accelerating decline in renal function
Gross haematuria with clot colic or haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: Progression is variable, with many PKD1 patients reaching end-stage kidney disease in mid-to-late adulthood while PKD2 disease progresses more slowly; blood pressure control and, in rapid progressors, vasopressin antagonism can delay kidney failure.
pitfalls: Applying adult ultrasound cyst criteria to young at-risk relatives, in whom absence of cysts does not exclude disease
Undertreating hypertension, a major modifiable driver of cardiovascular risk and progression
Offering aneurysm screening indiscriminately rather than to those with family history or specific risk
Missing cyst infection because standard imaging and cultures can be unremarkable
